content:
I have this proof:

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Dihedral

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : ∃ H : Subgroup G, ↑H = ⇑θ '' N ∧ H.Normal := by
  let C := ⇑θ '' N
  have mul_mem_H : ∀ {a b : G}, a ∈ C → b ∈ C → a * b ∈ C := by
    sorry -- snip
  have one_mem_H : 1 ∈ C := by
    sorry -- snip
  have inv_mem_H : ∀ {a : G}, a ∈ C → a⁻¹ ∈ C := by
    sorry -- snip
  let H' : Subgroup G := ⟨⟨⟨C, mul_mem_H⟩, one_mem_H⟩, inv_mem_H⟩
  let H : Subgroup G := {
      carrier := C
      mul_mem' := mul_mem_H
      one_mem' := one_mem_H
      inv_mem' := inv_mem_H
    }
  sorry -- snip

This compiles. But defining the subgroup I wanted was awkward.

The first problem I encountered was that I didn't know how to define a structure mid-proof; in an outer context, you have def ... where, but that isn't allowed inside an example.

The second problem was that I initially defined mul_mem_H and inv_mem_H with a and b bound explicitly ((a b : G)) rather than implicitly ({a b : G}). Despite these being exactly identical statements, making this error means that the construction of H and H' fails to typecheck. This was pretty simple to fix... but why in the world is this an issue?

The third problem is that, since Subgroup extends Submonoid extends Subsemigroup, you need to invoke all three of those constructors at once, and they require the various proofs involved to be nested backwards. Rather than constructing H' as ⟨C, mul_mem_H, one_mem_H, inv_mem_H⟩, which associates to the right, it's necessary to construct it as ⟨⟨⟨C, mul_mem_H⟩, one_mem_H⟩, inv_mem_H⟩, associated to the left and much, much harder to type.

Other classes with awkward "direct" constructors tend to supply a mk' method for convenient construction. (e.g. docs#MonoidHom.mk') Should Subgroup have one?
Hey! Could you spell out the mk' method you're suggesting? What is its signature?

def Subgroup.mk' {G : Type*} [Group G]
    (carrier : Set G)
    (mul_mem : ∀ a b : G, a ∈ carrier → b ∈ carrier → a * b ∈ carrier)
    (one_mem : 1 ∈ carrier)
    (inv_mem : ∀ a : G, a ∈ carrier → a⁻¹ ∈ carrier)
    : Subgroup G
(This isn't motivated so much by thinking that Subgroup.mk is asking for the wrong information as that it's asking for that information to be structured in an inconvenient way.)

I don't think making a, b explicit is a good idea, but IIUC you're inlining the Submonoid & Subsemigroup parts of Subgroup which seems useful to me.
However you can construct a Subgroup that way with both the { ... } and ⟨_, _, ...⟩ syntaxes, so I don't see the need for a named constructor.

def Subgroup.mk' {G : Type*} [Group G]
    (carrier : Set G)
    (mul_mem : ∀ a b : G, a ∈ carrier → b ∈ carrier → a * b ∈ carrier)
    (one_mem : 1 ∈ carrier)
    (inv_mem : ∀ a : G, a ∈ carrier → a⁻¹ ∈ carrier)
    : Subgroup G :=
  ⟨⟨⟨carrier, @mul_mem⟩, one_mem⟩, @inv_mem⟩
I do however wonder whether there's some attribute that will make Lean inline the extends parts in the constructor.

I don't understand your second point, the reason it's an issue is because they are different types. If instead of defining haves you just defined the theorems inline the issue wouldn't come up

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : ∃ H : Subgroup G, ↑H = ⇑θ '' N ∧ H.Normal := by
  use {
    carrier := ⇑θ '' N
    mul_mem' ha hb := by
      obtain ⟨y, _, _⟩ := ha
      obtain ⟨z, _, _⟩ := hb
      use y * z
      simp_all [Subgroup.mul_mem_cancel_right]
    one_mem' := by simp
    inv_mem' hx := by
      obtain ⟨y, _, _⟩ := hx
      use y⁻¹
      simp_all
  }

Michael said:

Other classes with awkward "direct" constructors tend to supply a mk' method for convenient construction. (e.g. docs#MonoidHom.mk')

This isn't because mk is awkward: docs#MonoidHom.mk' fills in map_one' if you have [Group G] [MulOneClass M], but in the general Monoid case you can't use it.
Also could this goal just be written (Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N).Normal to save this explicit construction?

What's the typing difference between ∀ x : G, x = 1 and ∀ {x : G}, x = 1? In one case, you're providing an instruction to the compiler to assume that an argument is present where it isn't written out. But the object in question is the same in both cases.

I don't think this has anything to do with the compiler, and yeah the difference is explicit vs implicit.
I don't understand the question

∀ x : G, x = 1 and ∀ {x : G}, x = 1 are equal, but a term of one type is not a drop-in replacement for a term of the other type because of elaboration. If the hole you have to fill is of type ∀ {x : G}, x = 1 then the way you have to fill it is to supply a term of type ? = 1, not a term of type ∀ x : G, x = 1.

i.e. you could derive this from (assuming youre not looking to do this as an exercise)

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : (Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N).Normal :=
  Subgroup.Normal.map ‹_› θ.toMonoidHom (by simp [MulEquiv.surjective])

could this goal just be written (Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N).Normal to save this explicit construction?

No, for the example I want two proofs: a proof that the image is a subgroup, and a proof that the subgroup is normal.

Michael said:

The first problem I encountered was that I didn't know how to define a structure mid-proof; in an outer context, you have def ... where, but that isn't allowed inside an example.

So in that situation one thing you might want to think is "perhaps the idiomatic thing to do is to make the definition outside of the proof", and that is indeed what the point of docs#Subgroup.map is.

Michael said:

could this goal just be written (Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N).Normal to save this explicit construction?

No, for the example I want two proofs: a proof that the image is a subgroup, and a proof that the subgroup is normal.

Subgroup carries data, that being the carrier set, and you can extract it from the statement.

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : (Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N).Normal :=
  Subgroup.Normal.map ‹_› θ.toMonoidHom (by simp [MulEquiv.surjective])

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : ↑(Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N) = θ '' N := by
  simp

Michael said:

The first problem I encountered was that I didn't know how to define a structure mid-proof; in an outer context, you have def ... where, but that isn't allowed inside an example.

But your definition of H is fine and the syntax is sensible. What is the problem with using the syntax you used for H?

The problem is that this syntax is a secret. The syntax itself is indeed fine. But I don't like having to use different methods of construction for different structures; why add the memory burden?

What's the point of the syntax for this declaration being radically different depending on whether you're at the top level of the file, or not?

I would also ask, if you think there's no problem with the definition of H, how does that suggest, as you implied, that defining H in that position is a mistake?

Vlad Tsyrklevich said:

Subgroup carries data, that being the carrier set, and you can extract it from the statement.

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : (Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N).Normal :=
  Subgroup.Normal.map ‹_› θ.toMonoidHom (by simp [MulEquiv.surjective])

example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : ↑(Subgroup.map θ.toMonoidHom N) = θ '' N := by
  simp

But the proof that the image of N is a subgroup of G isn't what's being demonstrated by your second example. It demonstrates that the image of N is the image of N. The proof that the image of N is a subgroup is, in your example, a corollary of Subgroup.map's proof that the image of any subgroup under a homomorphism is itself a subgroup. I want that proof to be explicit in the example.

Michael said:

The first problem I encountered was that I didn't know how to define a structure mid-proof; in an outer context, you have def ... where, but that isn't allowed inside an example.

Lean is sufficiently flexible that one can just fix this. I asked Claude to do so:

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Dihedral

syntax (name := letWhereTac) withPosition("let " ident " : " term
    " where" sepByIndentSemicolon(Lean.Parser.Term.structInstField)) : tactic

syntax (name := letIWhereTac) withPosition("letI " ident " : " term
    " where" sepByIndentSemicolon(Lean.Parser.Term.structInstField)) : tactic

macro_rules
  | `(tactic| let $x:ident : $t:term where $[$fields];*) => do
    let body ← `(Lean.Parser.Term.structInst| { $fields,* })
    `(tactic| let $x : $t := $(⟨body.raw⟩))
  | `(tactic| letI $x:ident : $t:term where $[$fields];*) => do
    let body ← `(Lean.Parser.Term.structInst| { $fields,* })
    `(tactic| letI $x : $t := $(⟨body.raw⟩))

-- now it works
example {G : Type*} [Group G] (θ : G ≃* G)
    (N : Subgroup G) [N.Normal]
    : ∃ H : Subgroup G, ↑H = ⇑θ '' N ∧ H.Normal := by
  let C := ⇑θ '' N
  have mul_mem_H : ∀ {a b : G}, a ∈ C → b ∈ C → a * b ∈ C := by
    sorry -- snip
  have one_mem_H : 1 ∈ C := by
    sorry -- snip
  have inv_mem_H : ∀ {a : G}, a ∈ C → a⁻¹ ∈ C := by
    sorry -- snip
  let H : Subgroup G where
      carrier := C
      mul_mem' := mul_mem_H
      one_mem' := one_mem_H
      inv_mem' := inv_mem_H
  sorry -- snip

Note: this is LLM-generated, I don't understand a word of it, and it might have deficiencies. But it does demonstrate the power of the system, and no doubt there will be a way to fix it correctly, even if this isn't it.

Michael said:

I would also ask, if you think there's no problem with the definition of H, how does that suggest, as you implied, that defining H in that position is a mistake?

I'm just saying that in this particular case, the way to define H in that position is to use the definition which already exists, and the way to get to that thought is to think "hmm, I need to construct the image of a subgroup under a group homomorphism -- is it likely that someone else needed this in the past?" rather than thinking "I need to construct the image of a subgroup under a group homomorphism so let's roll up my sleeves and get my hands dirty because I can see how to do this". I am suggesting that you "be more mathlib". The library is extremely thorough and the idea is that this is philosophy supposed to make your life easier.

Semantic search engines like https://leansearch.net/ , https://www.leanexplore.com/ , https://leandex.projectnumina.ai/ etc will accept natural language queries such as "image of a subgroup under a group homomorphism" and will guide you to these definitions.
